prompt:
Paddlesteamer Insurance, an Echuca insurer with 900 staff, wants to improve customer satisfaction. Its developers are building a portal that lets customers lodge and track claims online.

Explain the difference between a goal and an objective, using Paddlesteamer Insurance's claims portal as an example.

points.text: A goal is a broad, long-term aim that is not directly measurable, such as improving customer satisfaction
An objective is a specific, measurable target with a time frame that shows progress towards a goal
Gives an objective for the claims portal that has a measure and a time frame and supports the goal, e.g. reduce the average time to settle a claim from 15 working days to 7 within 12 months of launch

model: A goal is a broad, long-term aim that sets the organisation's direction but can't be measured directly. Paddlesteamer Insurance's goal is to improve customer satisfaction. An objective is a specific, measurable target with a deadline that shows progress towards a goal. An objective for the claims portal could be to reduce the average time taken to settle a claim from 15 working days to 7 within 12 months of the portal's launch. Meeting that target is evidence that the portal is helping to improve customer satisfaction.
mistake: An objective that restates the goal in other words ('customers will be happier with claims') earns no mark. It needs a figure to check against and a deadline.

prompt:
Tall Timber Outdoor, a Wodonga camping retailer with 300 staff and an online store, has the goal of becoming the most trusted outdoor retailer in north-east Victoria. Its developers keep the online store's source code, and a copy of the customer database, on a shared network drive that every employee can open.

Explain how this practice could stop Tall Timber Outdoor achieving its goal.

points.text: Identifies the vulnerability: every employee, not only the developers, can read, copy or change the source code and customer data
Describes a likely consequence, e.g. customer data leaked or code altered by an employee, deliberately or by accident, or reached by an attacker through any one compromised staff account
Links the consequence to the goal: exposed customer data would damage customers' trust and the retailer's reputation, working against becoming the most trusted outdoor retailer

model: Because the shared drive is open to every employee, anyone in the company, not just the developers, can read, copy or change the online store's source code and customers' personal details. An employee could leak customer records or alter the code, deliberately or by mistake, and an attacker who took over any single staff account would gain the same access. If customer data were exposed, customers would stop trusting Tall Timber Outdoor with their details, which works directly against its goal of being the most trusted outdoor retailer in north-east Victoria.

prompt:
Wirraway Plains Water, which supplies towns across northern Victoria and has 600 staff, has the goal of providing a reliable water supply to every customer. One of its objectives is to cut the average time taken to repair a burst water main from nine hours to five hours by June 2028. At present, call centre staff phone each burst-main report through to a supervisor, who then rings a repair crew.

The IT department can fund only one of these projects this year:

- **Project A**: a system that sends each burst-main report, with its location, from the call centre straight to the nearest repair crew's phones
- **Project B**: an online portal where customers can view and pay their water bills, requested by the finance manager and cheaper than Project A

Recommend which project Wirraway Plains Water should fund. Justify your recommendation with reference to the corporation's goal and objective.

points.text: Recommends Project A and explains how it supports the objective: reports reach a crew straight away instead of passing through a supervisor, so repairs start sooner and the average repair time falls towards five hours
Links Project A to the goal: shorter repairs mean customers are without water for less time, so the supply is more reliable
Explains why Project B is the weaker choice despite its lower cost: it makes paying bills more convenient but does nothing to shorten repairs or keep water flowing

model:
Wirraway Plains Water should fund Project A. At present each burst-main report is phoned through a supervisor before a crew hears about it. Sending the report and its location straight to the nearest crew removes that delay, so repairs can start sooner. This directly supports the objective of cutting the average repair time from nine hours to five.

Shorter repairs mean customers are without water for less time, which serves the goal of a reliable supply for every customer. Project B would make paying bills more convenient, and it costs less, but it does nothing to shorten repairs or keep water flowing, so it doesn't serve this goal or objective.
mistake: A recommendation needs a choice and a reason tied to the scenario. 'Project A is more useful' earns little; link it to the nine-to-five-hour objective and the reliable-supply goal, and say why Project B doesn't serve them.

prompt:
Numbat Legal, a Melbourne law firm with 150 staff, needs a document management system that will store confidential client files. Its IT team of three maintains the office network and laptops but has never built a large program. The system could be developed in-house by the IT team, or by an external software developer.

Recommend one of these options for Numbat Legal. Justify your recommendation by explaining one advantage and one disadvantage of the option you choose, and how the firm could manage that disadvantage.

points.text: Recommends an option and gives an advantage of it that applies to Numbat Legal, e.g. external: specialist developers have the skills the three-person IT team lacks; in-house: confidential client files stay within the firm
Explains why that advantage matters for the firm, e.g. a system built by experienced developers is less likely to contain flaws that expose client files; or no third party ever sees client documents

Identifies a disadvantage of the chosen option that applies to the firm, e.g. external: the developer's staff may see confidential client files; in-house: the team's lack of development experience could make the system slow to build or insecure

Describes a realistic way to manage that disadvantage, e.g. a contract with confidentiality and security terms and invented test files; or hiring or training an experienced developer and reviewing the code

model: I recommend that Numbat Legal have the system developed externally. The firm's three IT staff maintain the network but have never built a large program, whereas a specialist developer has the skills and experience to build a document management system. This matters because a system built by inexperienced staff is more likely to contain security flaws that could expose confidential client files. The disadvantage is that the developer's staff may need access to the firm's systems and could see confidential client files. The firm can manage this with a contract that includes confidentiality and security obligations, by giving the developer invented test documents instead of real client files, and by reviewing the delivered code before it goes live.
mistake: Either option can earn full marks. The marks come from reasons tied to Numbat Legal (the three-person IT team, the confidential client files), not from the choice itself.

prompt:
Tumbleweed Couriers, a Dandenong delivery company with 200 staff, had its booking app built by an external developer. The contract didn't mention the source code, and the developer has refused to hand it over. A security flaw has now been found in the app.

Explain one consequence of this situation for Tumbleweed Couriers, and state one contract term that would have prevented it.

points.text: Explains a consequence: without the source code, Tumbleweed Couriers can't fix the security flaw itself or have another developer fix it, so the flaw stays open to attack, or it must pay the original developer on that developer's terms
States a contract term: the source code and its documentation are owned by, or handed over to, Tumbleweed Couriers when the project ends

model: Without the source code, Tumbleweed Couriers can't patch the security flaw itself or hire another developer to do it, so the app stays open to attack until the original developer agrees to fix it, on whatever terms and price that developer sets. The contract should have stated that the source code and its documentation belong to Tumbleweed Couriers and are handed over when the project ends.

prompt:
Bushwren Health Fund, a Geelong health insurer with 400 staff, has six developers who built and maintain its membership system. It now needs a module that records each member's claims, calculates the benefit paid for each claim and pays it into the member's bank account. The benefit rules change every April.

The board has decided to have the module developed in-house rather than by an external software firm. Justify the board's decision.

points.text: The fund's own developers already know the membership system that the module must work with, whereas an external firm would first have to learn it
The benefit rules change every April, and in-house developers can make each change when it is needed, without negotiating and paying for a new contract each time

Members' claims, which show the health services they used, and their bank account details stay within the fund, handled only by its own staff under its own security controls rather than shared with a third party

model:
The fund's six developers built the membership system, so they already understand the system the new module must work with. An external firm would have to learn it first, which adds time and cost.

The benefit rules change every April. In-house developers can update the module each time the rules change, as soon as the change is needed, instead of the fund negotiating and paying for new work under a contract every year.

The module will hold members' claims, which show the health services they have used, and their bank account details. Developing it in-house means only the fund's own staff handle that data, under its own security controls, so it isn't exposed to a third party's staff or systems.
mistake: Justify needs reasons tied to the scenario. 'In-house gives more control' earns little unless it says what the fund controls, such as the April rule changes or members' claims and bank details, and why that matters here.

prompt:
Pardalote Health Software, a Bendigo company with 120 staff, develops a patient portal for medical clinics. Its current development practices are shown in the table.

Identify two vulnerabilities in these practices and explain a risk that each creates for Pardalote Health Software.

points.text: Identifies a first vulnerability from the table, e.g. development, testing and release all happen on the live portal's server; the six developers share one administrator login; new features are tested with a copy of real patient data; or third-party libraries are not updated promptly

Explains a risk the first vulnerability creates for Pardalote, e.g. an untested change takes the portal offline or exposes patient records; no action can be traced to one developer and one person's access can't be removed alone; a breach of the less protected test copy exposes patients' health information; or attackers exploit publicly known library flaws
Identifies a second, different vulnerability from the table
Explains a risk the second vulnerability creates (as in the examples above)

model: First, the developers write, test and release code on the server that runs the live patient portal. An untested change or a developer's mistake goes straight to the live system, so it could take the portal offline for clinics or expose patient records to the wrong users. Second, new features are tested with a copy of the live patient database. Patients' health information is then held in a test environment with weaker controls and more people using it, so anyone with test access can see it, and a breach of the test copy would expose it.
mistake: Naming a practice earns the identify mark only. The second mark needs the harm it could cause to Pardalote's portal or its patients' data.

figures.title: Development practices at Pardalote Health Software
rows: Developers write, test and release code on the server that runs the live patient portal
The six developers share one administrator login
New features are tested with a copy of the live patient database
Third-party libraries are updated when a developer has spare time

prompt:
Hollowlog Media, a Melbourne app developer with 60 staff, did not disable the accounts of three developers who left the company last year. The accounts can still log in to the company's code repository.

Explain why these accounts are a vulnerability for Hollowlog Media.

points.text: The former developers can still read, copy or change Hollowlog Media's code although they no longer have any legitimate need for access
Nobody is using or watching the accounts, so an attacker who obtains one of their passwords can get into the repository with little chance of being noticed

model: The three former developers can still log in to the repository and read, copy or change Hollowlog Media's code, even though they no longer work there and have no legitimate need for access. Because nobody uses or monitors these accounts, an attacker who obtained one of their passwords could also get into the repository and alter or steal code with little chance of being noticed.

prompt:
Ironpot Fresh, a Wodonga online grocery delivery company with 140 staff, runs its development work and its live customer database on the same server. The database holds customers' names, home addresses, phone numbers and order histories. So that developers can work from home, the server accepts logins from anywhere on the internet with only a username and password.

Explain how these two weaknesses together put customers' personal data at risk.

points.text: Because logins are accepted from anywhere with only a password, anyone who guesses, steals or tricks a developer out of their password can log in from outside the company
Because development and the live database share one server, getting into the development environment also reaches the live customer data

States the consequence for customers: their names, home addresses, phone numbers and order histories could be copied, changed or deleted, exposing them to scams and damaging their trust in the company

model:
Because the server accepts logins from anywhere with only a username and password, anyone who guesses or steals a developer's password, for example through a fake login email, can log in from outside the company with nothing else to stop them.

Because the development work and the live customer database share the same server, logging in to do development work also reaches the live customer records. Together, one stolen password could let an attacker copy, change or delete customers' names, home addresses, phone numbers and order histories. Customers could then be targeted by scams that use their real details, and they would lose trust in Ironpot Fresh.
mistake: Describing each weakness on its own misses 'together'. Show how the first gives an attacker a way in, and how the second means that way in leads straight to live customer data.

prompt:
Mallee Rise Water, a regional water corporation with 350 staff, has eight in-house developers. They log in to every system with a username and password, and every developer has administrator access to the live billing system, which stores customers' names, addresses and bank account details.

Recommend two software security controls that would better protect the billing data, and explain how each would protect it.

points.text: Recommends a first software control, e.g. multi-factor authentication for developer logins; least privilege through identity and access management; encryption of the stored billing data; or separate development, testing and production environments

Explains how the first control protects the billing data, e.g. a stolen password alone no longer reaches the system; fewer accounts can read or change bank details; copied bank details can't be read without the key; or developers work with invented data and don't need live access
Recommends a second, different control
Explains how the second control protects the billing data (as in the examples above)

model: First, Mallee Rise Water should require multi-factor authentication, such as a password plus a code from an authenticator app, for every developer login. A developer's stolen or guessed password would then not be enough on its own to reach customers' bank details. Second, it should apply least privilege through identity and access management, giving each developer only the access their role needs. Most developers would lose administrator access to the live billing system, so far fewer accounts could read or change customers' bank details, whether through misuse, error or a compromised account.
mistake: Recommending 'strong passwords' adds little here: Mallee Rise already uses passwords. Recommend a control that changes the current situation, and say what it protects.

prompt:
Bottlebrush Software's development servers and backup drives sit on an open shelf in an unlocked storeroom beside the staff kitchen in its Ballarat office. Visitors and cleaners use the kitchen every day.

Describe two physical security controls that would protect the servers and backup drives.

points.text: A lock on the storeroom, such as swipe-card or key access, so that only authorised staff can enter
CCTV or an entry log for the storeroom, so that anyone who enters is recorded and can be identified
Backup drives kept in a locked safe or stored off-site, so that they can't be taken or destroyed along with the servers

model: Bottlebrush Software should fit a swipe-card lock to the storeroom so that only authorised staff can enter, keeping visitors and cleaners away from the servers. It should also keep the backup drives in a locked safe or at a separate site, so that a single theft, fire or flood in the storeroom can't take both the servers and their backups.

prompt:
Tarilta Homewares, a Castlemaine online homewares retailer with 200 staff, keeps its web store's code in a version control system. Any of its five developers can merge a change into the live code without anyone else checking it. Last month, an attacker who had stolen one developer's password added code that copied customers' card details to an outside server. The change went live straight away and wasn't noticed for a week.

1. Explain how requiring a code review before every merge could have prevented this harm.
2. Explain how the version control system helps Tarilta Homewares now that the attack has been found.

points.text: Part 1: a second developer must examine and approve each change before it is merged, so code sending card details to an outside server would very likely have been noticed
Part 1: the change would have been blocked before going live, so no card details would have been copied; holding one developer's account, the attacker couldn't approve their own change

Part 2: the version history shows exactly which lines were added, from which account and when, so the team can find all of the attacker's code, know which account was compromised and work out which week of orders was exposed
Part 2: the team can roll the web store back to the last version before the malicious change, or revert that change, removing the attacker's code quickly

model:
1. If every merge needed a code review, a second developer would have had to read and approve the attacker's change before it reached the live store. Code that sends customers' card details to an outside server is unusual and would very likely have been spotted. The attacker held only one developer's account, so they couldn't approve their own change, and it would have been blocked before any card details were copied.

2. The version control system recorded the change. Its history shows exactly which lines were added, from which developer's account and when, so the team can find every part of the attacker's code, lock the compromised account and work out which week of orders was exposed. The team can also roll the web store back to the last version before the change, or revert that change, removing the malicious code quickly.
mistake: Version control doesn't stop a malicious change; it records it. Credit comes from saying what the history shows and what rolling back achieves.

prompt:
Pepper Creek Vets, a Bendigo veterinary group with 140 staff, is designing an app in which pet owners book appointments and vets record treatments. Part of the design is shown in the DFD. The developers are threat modelling the design.

Identify one threat to the data shown in the DFD. Explain how the developers should mitigate it, and how they could test that the mitigation works.

points.text: Identifies a threat tied to a named element of the DFD, e.g. booking_request intercepted in transit; someone posing as a vet sends false treatment_notes; unauthorised access to the Medical records store
Explains the harm the threat would cause, e.g. owners' personal details exposed; pets' medical records altered or disclosed
Describes a control that mitigates that threat, e.g. encrypting the flow in transit; multi-factor authentication for vets; role-based access and encryption for the Medical records store
Describes a test that would show the mitigation works, e.g. trying to submit treatment notes with a correct password but no second factor and confirming it is refused

model: One threat is that someone who has stolen a vet's password could pose as that vet and send false `treatment_notes` to process 2, altering pets' records in the Medical records store. Wrong treatment records could lead to a pet being given the wrong medication. The developers should mitigate this by requiring multi-factor authentication for vets, so a password alone can't be used to record a treatment. To test the mitigation, they would try to log in as a test vet with the correct password but without the second factor, and confirm that the app refuses to accept any treatment notes.
mistake: A threat that isn't tied to the diagram, such as 'hackers', earns little. Name the flow, process or store at risk and what could happen to it.

prompt:
The Pepper Creek Vets developers want to leave threat modelling until the app has been released, so that they can finish building it sooner.

Explain why they should carry out threat modelling during design instead.

points.text: Threats found during design can be removed by changing the design, which is cheaper and faster than reworking the code of the released app
Weaknesses are dealt with before release, so pet owners' personal details and pets' medical records are never exposed through the live app

model: If the developers model threats during design, any weakness they find can be removed by changing the design before code is written, which is far cheaper and quicker than reworking the released app. It also means the controls are in place from the first day the app is live, so pet owners' personal details and pets' medical records aren't exposed to attackers while the developers catch up.

prompt:
The Shire of Wandarrie, a council with 380 staff, has an app that residents use to register their pets. The council now wants the app to update each pet's record held by an outside microchip registry, sending the owner's name, address and phone number. This new feature is process 2 and its flows in the DFD. The development team completed a threat model for the app last year.

Explain why the team must update its threat model before building this feature. In your answer, identify one new threat the feature introduces and a control that would mitigate it.

points.text: Explains why the model must be updated, e.g. the feature adds a new process and new flows, including owners' personal details leaving the council for an outside organisation, which last year's threat model never considered; or updating it before building lets controls be designed in, which is cheaper than changing finished code

Identifies a new threat tied to process 2 or its flows, e.g. owner_details intercepted on the way to the registry; an attacker posing as the registry to collect owners' details or return a false update_status

Describes a control that mitigates the threat identified, e.g. encrypting owner_details in transit; confirming the registry's identity before any details are sent; sending only the fields the registry needs

model:
Last year's threat model covered only the elements the app had then. The new feature adds process 2, the microchip registry as a new external entity, and three new flows. For the first time residents' names, addresses and phone numbers leave the council for an outside organisation. The existing model never considered these elements, so their threats have not been identified or mitigated. Updating the model before building means any controls can be designed in, rather than added to finished code.

One new threat is that `owner_details` could be intercepted as they travel over the internet to the microchip registry, exposing pet owners' personal details. The team should mitigate this by encrypting `owner_details` in transit, so intercepted details can't be read.
mistake: A threat that isn't tied to the new feature, such as 'hackers could attack the app', earns little. Name the new flow, process or entity and what could happen to it.

figures.title: DFD (part): Shire of Wandarrie pet registration
figures.caption: Process 2 and its flows are the new feature.

prompt:
Keelback Logistics, a Bendigo freight company, employs six developers who maintain its parcel-tracking system. The system stores customers' names, addresses and phone numbers. Management wants to evaluate how secure the team's development practices are.

Propose two criteria Keelback Logistics could use to evaluate the security of its development practices. For each criterion, describe the evidence that would show whether it is met.

points.text: Criterion 1: a specific, checkable standard for one development practice, e.g. every change to the tracking system is approved by a second developer before it is merged
Evidence for criterion 1 that directly shows whether it is met, e.g. the repository's merge history shows an approval by a developer other than the author for each change
Criterion 2: a specific, checkable standard for a different practice, e.g. test environments contain no identifiable customer names, addresses or phone numbers
Evidence for criterion 2, e.g. an inspection of a sample of test database records confirms that customer details are made up or de-identified

model:
Criterion 1: Every change to the parcel-tracking system's code is reviewed and approved by a second developer before it is merged. Evidence: the repository's merge history for the last three months, checked to confirm that each merged change was approved by a developer other than its author.

Criterion 2: Test environments contain no identifiable customer names, addresses or phone numbers. Evidence: an inspection of a sample of records in the test database, confirming that the customer details are made up or de-identified rather than copied from the live system.
mistake: Criteria such as 'the system is secure' can't be checked, and evidence such as 'ask the developers' is opinion. Name a specific practice, and a record, log or test that shows whether it happens.

prompt:
Kunzea Home Loans, a Warragul lender, has five developers who maintain its loan application website. Applicants upload payslips and bank statements through the website. The IT manager, Petra, has drafted two criteria for evaluating the security of the team's development practices:

- **Criterion 1**: Our developers take security seriously.
- **Criterion 2**: The loan application website has a secure login page.

Explain why each criterion is unsuitable for evaluating the security of Kunzea Home Loans' development practices.

points.text: Criterion 1 is an opinion that names no development practice, so it isn't specific or measurable

No record, log or test could show whether criterion 1 is met, so the evaluation couldn't reach a reliable judgement, e.g. the developers could believe they take security seriously while sharing one login
Criterion 2 judges a feature of the finished website, not the practices used to develop it

The login page could be secure while the practices are weak, e.g. a password written in the code or real applicants' payslips used for testing, so meeting criterion 2 wouldn't show that the practices are secure

model:
Criterion 1 is an opinion. It doesn't name any development practice, so there is nothing specific to check. No record, log or test could show whether it is met: the five developers could all believe they take security seriously while sharing one repository login. The evaluation couldn't reach a reliable judgement.

Criterion 2 judges the finished website, not how Kunzea Home Loans develops it. The login page could be secure while the team's practices are weak, for example if a database password is written into the code, or if real applicants' payslips and bank statements are copied into the test environment. Meeting criterion 2 wouldn't show that the development practices are secure.
mistake: Calling a criterion 'too vague' earns only part of the marks. Explain the consequence: no evidence could show whether it is met. Criterion 2 can look acceptable because it mentions security, but it judges the product, not the practices used to build it.

prompt:
Hakea Legal Systems, a Ballarat company with 14 developers, builds case-management software that law firms use to store confidential client files. In the past year:

- a contractor copied part of the source code three weeks after her contract ended, using her repository account, which was still active
- a developer merged a change that switched off the password check on the software's administrator page for testing, and the change reached the live software unnoticed for two weeks.

The security officer, Aiko, will evaluate the team's development practices against these two criteria:

- **A**: Repository access is removed on the day each staff member or contractor leaves.
- **B**: Every change is approved by a developer other than its author before it is merged.

Justify Aiko's choice of criteria.

points.text: A is linked to a real risk at Hakea: the former contractor's still-active account let her copy confidential source code after she left
A can be checked with evidence, e.g. comparing each person's leaving date with the date their account was disabled in the access logs
B is linked to a real risk at Hakea: a second developer reviewing the change would be likely to notice the switched-off password check before it reached the live software
B can be checked with evidence, e.g. the repository's merge history shows who approved each change
Both criteria judge how the software is developed rather than features of the finished software, so they suit an evaluation of development practices

model:
Criterion A targets a weakness that has already caused harm at Hakea. The contractor's account stayed active after her contract ended, and she used it to copy source code for software that handles law firms' confidential files. A is also checkable: Aiko can compare each person's leaving date in staff and contract records with the date their account was disabled in the access logs.

Criterion B targets the second incident. The change that switched off the administrator password check was merged by its author without anyone else seeing it. A second developer reviewing it would be likely to notice the missing check before it reached the live software. B is also checkable, because the repository's merge history records who approved each change, so Aiko can confirm that no one approved their own work.
mistake: Saying what each criterion checks isn't a justification. Link each criterion to the incident at Hakea that shows why it matters, and say what evidence would show whether it is met.

prompt:
Bristlebird Allied Health, a private clinic in Warrnambool, has engaged Tawnyhill Apps, an external developer, to build a booking and treatment-notes app. The app will store patients' contact details and treatment notes. Tawnyhill Apps plans to include an open-source calendar library in the app.

Identify two Acts that apply to this project and explain how each affects the way Tawnyhill Apps develops the app.

points.text: Identifies a privacy Act that applies to patients' information: the Health Records Act 2001 (Vic) or the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth)

Explains its effect on development, applied to the app, e.g. the app must protect treatment notes from unauthorised access (such as by encrypting them and letting only authorised clinic staff view them), collect only the information the clinic needs, and be tested without real patient records
Identifies a second Act: the Copyright Act 1968 (Cth) for the calendar library, or the other privacy Act
Explains its effect on development, e.g. Tawnyhill Apps follows the library's licence conditions, such as keeping its copyright notice, and acknowledges it in the documentation

model:
The Health Records Act 2001 (Vic) applies because the app stores treatment notes, which are health information held by a private Victorian clinic. The app must let the clinic meet the Act, so Tawnyhill Apps must build it to protect the notes from unauthorised access, for example by encrypting them and letting only authorised clinic staff view them, and it should test the app with made-up patient records rather than real ones.

The Copyright Act 1968 (Cth) applies to the open-source calendar library, which is protected by copyright even though it is freely available. Tawnyhill Apps must follow the library's licence conditions, such as keeping its copyright notice, and acknowledge the library in the app's documentation.
mistake: Naming an Act without linking it to the app earns little. Say which data or code the Act covers and what Tawnyhill Apps must do because of it.

prompt:
Sandstone Freight Systems in Dandenong has six developers. All of them log in to their laptops and to the build server with administrator accounts, and the build server's operating system has not been updated for 14 months.

Identify two Essential Eight strategies that the team is not following, and explain how applying each would reduce the risk to Sandstone Freight Systems' code and data.

points.text: Identifies restrict administrative privileges
Explains: developers use standard accounts for daily work, so a stolen login or malware running under a developer's account can't change settings or install software across the build server
Identifies patch operating systems
Explains: updating the build server's operating system closes known vulnerabilities that attackers could use to access or alter the code it builds

model:
Restrict administrative privileges: the developers should use standard accounts for everyday work, with administrator rights given only to the few staff who need them. If a developer's login is stolen or malware runs on a laptop, it can't install software or change settings across the build server, which limits the damage to Sandstone's code.

Patch operating systems: the build server's operating system should be updated promptly. After 14 months without updates it has known vulnerabilities that attackers can use, and patching closes them, reducing the chance that the code built on the server is accessed or altered.
mistake: Naming 'patching' without saying what is patched, or 'admin rights' without saying who loses them, doesn't apply the strategy to the scenario.

prompt:
Riflebird Ticketing, a Melbourne company covered by the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth), sells concert tickets through its website and stores customers' names, email addresses, phone numbers and purchase histories. A review of its development practices found that:

- administrator accounts on the web server are protected by a password only
- the web server's operating system is missing nine months of security updates
- the customer database is backed up weekly, but no one has ever tried restoring a backup.

The operations manager says there is no point adopting the Essential Eight, because it is not law. Justify why Riflebird Ticketing should adopt the Essential Eight, with reference to the review's findings.

points.text: Although the Essential Eight is voluntary guidance, the Privacy Act requires Riflebird to take reasonable steps to protect the personal information it holds, and the Essential Eight gives it a recognised, prioritised set of strategies for taking those steps
Multi-factor authentication for the administrator accounts: a stolen or guessed password alone would no longer let an attacker into the web server and customer database
Patching operating systems: updating the web server closes the known vulnerabilities left open by nine months without updates, which attackers could use to break in
Regular backups, with restores tested: the weekly backups may not work, and testing them means customer data could be recovered after ransomware or an accidental deletion

Links the strategies to Riflebird's obligations: a breach likely to cause serious harm would have to be reported to the affected customers and the Australian Information Commissioner, damaging their trust

model:
The Essential Eight isn't law, but the Privacy Act requires Riflebird to take reasonable steps to protect the customers' personal information it holds. The Act doesn't list which controls to use, and the Essential Eight gives a recognised, prioritised set of strategies that match the weaknesses the review found.

Multi-factor authentication would protect the administrator accounts, so a stolen or guessed password alone could no longer be used to reach the web server and the customer database. Patching operating systems would close the known vulnerabilities that have built up in the nine months since the web server was last updated, which attackers look for. Regular backups, with restores tested, would mean that customer data could actually be recovered after ransomware or an accidental deletion; at present no one knows whether the weekly backups work.

Together these make a breach of customers' details much less likely. A breach likely to cause serious harm would have to be reported to the affected customers and the Australian Information Commissioner, which would damage their trust in Riflebird.
mistake: Calling the Essential Eight 'best practice' doesn't justify adopting it. Name each strategy, the finding at Riflebird it fixes, and the harm it prevents.

prompt:
Galah Creek Software, a small Geelong company, is building a membership app for a chain of gyms. To meet a tight deadline, its developers:
- paste AI-generated functions into the app without reviewing them
- copy code from online forums without recording where it came from
- test the app using the gyms' real member records.

Explain two ethical issues raised by Galah Creek Software's development practices.

points.text: Identifies an ethical issue from the scenario, e.g. over-reliance on AI-generated code that hasn't been reviewed
Explains the harm and who bears it, e.g. the functions may contain errors or vulnerabilities that expose members' details, while Galah Creek remains responsible for the code it releases
Identifies a second ethical issue, e.g. using real member records for testing, or not acknowledging code copied from forums

Explains the harm, e.g. members didn't agree to their data being used for testing and it is more exposed in a test environment; or authors aren't credited and the code's licence and security can't be checked

model:
Over-reliance on AI-generated code: the developers paste in functions they haven't reviewed, so the app may contain errors or security vulnerabilities that expose gym members' personal details. Galah Creek remains responsible for that code, and the gyms and their members carry the risk without knowing it.

Using real member records for testing: members gave their details to join a gym, not to have them used to test software. Test environments usually have weaker controls, so the records are more likely to be exposed. Made-up test data would avoid this harm.
mistake: Stating that a practice is 'unethical' without saying who is harmed, and how, earns little. Name the stakeholder, such as the gym members, and the harm to them.

prompt:
Two years ago Oskar, a developer at Eurabbie Plumbing Supplies in Geelong, copied a date-checking function from a public code repository into the company's online ordering app. He deleted the original author's comments and didn't record where the function came from. This month, a security flaw was announced in that function, and its author released a fixed version.

Explain why Oskar's failure to acknowledge the reused function is an ethical issue. Refer to the security flaw in your answer.

points.text: Deleting the author's comments presents someone else's work as Oskar's own and denies the author credit, which is dishonest to the author and to his employer
With no record of the function's source, the team may not realise that the announced flaw affects the ordering app, or know that a fixed version exists
The app may therefore stay vulnerable, putting customers' orders and details at risk without their knowledge

model:
By deleting the author's comments, Oskar presents the function as his own work. The author loses the credit, and Eurabbie Plumbing Supplies is misled about who wrote its code.

Because Oskar didn't record where the function came from, no one at Eurabbie can link the announced flaw to the ordering app or know that a fixed version exists. The app may stay vulnerable for months, and the customers whose orders and details it holds carry that risk without knowing it.
mistake: Calling it 'plagiarism' earns only part of the marks. Explain the harm: here, no one can link the announced flaw to the app, so customers stay exposed.

prompt:
A fault in the new invoicing module at a Horsham farm supplies business emailed each of 40 customers an invoice belonging to a different customer. Each invoice showed that customer's name, address, phone number and purchase history. The developer, Freya, has fixed the fault. The manager wants to say nothing to the customers whose invoices were sent to someone else, because the fault is fixed and telling them could harm the business's reputation.

Justify why the business should tell those customers what happened.

points.text: Fixing the fault stops new errors but doesn't undo the disclosure: 40 customers' details are already in other people's inboxes
Once told, the affected customers can protect themselves, e.g. by being wary of scam calls or emails that use their details
Hiding the mistake is dishonest to customers who trusted the business with their details; telling them openly is more likely to keep their trust than having them find out later

model:
Fixing the fault stops it happening again, but it doesn't undo what has already happened: 40 customers' names, addresses, phone numbers and purchase histories are in other people's inboxes. Those customers are the ones at risk, and only if they are told can they protect themselves, for example by being wary of scam calls or emails that quote their details.

Saying nothing would also be dishonest. The customers trusted the business with their details, and if they later found out that the business had hidden the mistake, they would lose far more trust in it than if they had been told openly.
mistake: Saying 'it is the right thing to do' doesn't justify the decision, and neither does 'the law says so', because the scenario doesn't say whether a notification law covers this business. Give reasons tied to the scenario: the details are already exposed, and only customers who are told can protect themselves.

prompt:
Boobook Surveying, a Horsham company, has three developers who build its survey-processing software. Each developer keeps a full copy of the source code on a laptop that they take home and to job sites, and the laptops' drives are not encrypted. The office server that holds the code repository and the client database is backed up once a month.

For each of these two practices, propose a measure that would reduce the risk, and explain how it reduces the risk.

points.text: Unencrypted laptops: proposes encrypting each laptop's whole drive (encryption at rest)
Explains: if a laptop is lost or stolen, the source code on it can't be read without the key, so the thief gets the hardware but not the code or any secrets in it
Monthly backups: proposes automatic backups at least daily, optionally kept offline or off-site with restores tested
Explains: if the server fails, is attacked or files are deleted by mistake, the code and client data can be restored with at most a day's work lost, instead of up to a month's

model:
Unencrypted laptops: Boobook should encrypt the whole drive of every developer's laptop. If a laptop is lost or stolen at a job site, the source code on it can't be read without the key, so the thief gets the hardware but not the company's code.

Monthly backups: Boobook should back up the server automatically every night. If the server fails, is hit by ransomware or files are deleted by mistake, the repository and client database can be restored with at most one day's work lost, rather than up to a month's.
mistake: Encrypting data in transit doesn't protect a stolen laptop. The code on its drive is stored data, so it needs encryption at rest.

prompt:
Jonah, a developer at Ferncastle Lending in Bendigo, wrote the login module below. The arrays `users` and `passwords` hold each staff member's username and password, and `passwords[i]` belongs to `users[i]`. No staff member has the username `guest`. Arrays are indexed from 0.

State what the module displays when the username `guest` and the password `Kookaburra99` are entered. Explain the weakness this shows, and propose two measures that would reduce or remove the risk.

points.text: States the output: Welcome guest
Explains the weakness: lines 2 and 11 hard-code a master password that logs anyone in under any username, and anyone who can read the source code or its version history can see it
Measure 1, e.g. delete line 2 and remove the master password test from line 11, so that every login must match a real staff account
Measure 2, e.g. require a second developer to review every change before it is merged, or scan code for hard-coded secrets, so that back doors and passwords in code are caught before release

model:
The module displays **Welcome guest**. No staff member is called guest, so `found` stays FALSE, but line 11 also accepts the master password on its own. This is a hard-coded back door: anyone who knows Kookaburra99 can log in under any username, and anyone who can read the source code or the repository's history can find it on line 2.

Measure 1: delete line 2 and change line 11 to `IF found = TRUE THEN`, so that every login must match a real staff account. Any administrator who needs access should have their own account, protected by multi-factor authentication.

Measure 2: require a second developer to review every change before it is merged, so that back doors and hard-coded passwords like this one are caught before the module is released.
mistake: The weakness isn't only that a password can be read in the code. Line 11 accepts the master password with any username, so it bypasses the account check completely.

figures.title: Login module
figures.code:
BEGIN
    masterPassword ← "Kookaburra99"
    INPUT username
    INPUT password
    found ← FALSE
    FOR i ← 0 TO LENGTH(users) - 1
        IF users[i] = username AND passwords[i] = password THEN
            found ← TRUE
        ENDIF
    ENDFOR
    IF found = TRUE OR password = masterPassword THEN
        DISPLAY "Welcome " + username
    ELSE
        DISPLAY "Login failed"
    ENDIF
END

prompt:
Sunita is one of six developers at a Sale company that builds booking software for camping grounds. All six developers can log in to the live booking database with full rights. Last month Sunita ran a clean-up script, meant for the test database, against the live database by mistake, and it deleted 2,000 upcoming bookings. The latest backup was a week old, so staff spent three days re-entering bookings from customers' emails.

Explain how two measures would reduce the risk of this happening again. For each measure, state whether it reduces the likelihood or the impact of a repeat.

points.text: Measure 1 is specific to the scenario, e.g. remove developers' direct access to the live database so that only an approved release process can change it, or give the live and test databases separate logins so that a script aimed at the test database can't connect to the live one
Explains how measure 1 reduces the risk and classifies it correctly, e.g. a script run by mistake can no longer change live bookings, which reduces the likelihood
Measure 2 is specific to the scenario, e.g. automatic backups of the live database at least nightly, with restores tested
Explains how measure 2 reduces the risk and classifies it correctly, e.g. deleted bookings could be restored with at most a day's loss instead of three days of re-entry, which reduces the impact

model:
Measure 1: remove the developers' direct access to the live booking database, so that changes reach it only through an approved release process. A clean-up script run by mistake would then be refused by the live database, so this reduces the likelihood of bookings being deleted again.

Measure 2: back up the live database automatically every night, and test each month that a backup can be restored. If bookings were deleted again, they could be restored from the previous night's backup, losing at most a day's bookings instead of a week's, and staff wouldn't spend three days re-entering them. This reduces the impact of a repeat.
mistake: 'Be more careful' isn't a measure, and backing up more often reduces the impact of a repeat, not its likelihood. Say what changes, and classify each measure correctly.

prompt:
Myrtle Beech Rostering, a Ballarat company, builds rostering software for aged-care providers. An evaluation of its development practices produced the findings shown.

Recommend two improvements to Myrtle Beech Rostering's development practices. Justify each recommendation with reference to the findings.

points.text: Recommendation 1: a specific action that addresses one finding, e.g. require a second developer to approve every change before it is merged
Justification 1, linked to the finding, e.g. developers now merge their own changes unchecked, so flaws such as hard-coded passwords reach the live system; a reviewer would catch them

Recommendation 2: a specific action that addresses a different finding, e.g. disable the former developers' accounts and review access regularly; move the database password into a protected secrets store and change it; or use made-up staff records for testing
Justification 2, linked to the finding, e.g. the former developers no longer need access, and their accounts could be used to copy or change the code without anyone noticing

model:
Recommendation 1: Myrtle Beech Rostering should require a second developer to review and approve every change before it can be merged. At present developers merge their own changes, so errors and security flaws, such as the live database password written into three source files, reach the live system unnoticed. A reviewer would catch these before release.

Recommendation 2: Myrtle Beech Rostering should immediately disable the repository accounts of the two developers who left in June, and review all access each month. Former staff no longer need access, and their accounts could be used to copy or change the rostering code without anyone noticing.
mistake: A recommendation that could apply to any company, such as 'use better security', earns little. Name the finding it fixes and the risk it removes.

figures.title: Evaluation findings
rows: Developers merge their own changes without review
The live database password is written in three source files
Two developers who left in June still have repository access
The test system uses a full copy of live staff records

prompt:
Antechinus Credit Co-operative in Traralgon lets its developers paste customers' account records into a public AI chatbot to help them find the causes of errors.

Recommend one change to this practice. Justify your recommendation, and describe how the co-operative could check that the change is being followed.

points.text: Recommends a specific change, e.g. a rule that developers never enter real customer records into AI tools and use made-up or de-identified records instead
Justifies it: pasting real account records into a public chatbot discloses customers' personal information to an outside party, where it may be stored and is beyond the co-operative's control
Describes a check that uses evidence, e.g. provide an approved AI tool and review its prompt logs regularly for real customer names or account numbers

model:
The co-operative should adopt a rule that developers never paste real customer records into AI tools, and use made-up or de-identified records when they need help finding the cause of an error. At present, customers' account details are being disclosed to an outside company, where they may be stored and reused beyond the co-operative's control. This exposes customers to harm and breaks their trust.

To check that the rule is followed, the co-operative could provide an approved AI tool and review its prompt logs each month, confirming that no real customer names or account numbers appear in them.

prompt:
Sittella Insurance, a Ballarat insurer with 600 staff, has 20 developers who use an AI coding assistant. Last month a junior developer committed an AI-generated function without reading it. The function let logged-in customers view other customers' claims, and a customer reported the flaw two weeks after release. The team leader wants to ban AI coding assistants. The developers say the assistant saves each of them several hours a week, and the team is behind schedule on its new claims app.

Recommend whether Sittella Insurance should ban AI coding assistants or allow them with rules. Justify your recommendation.

points.text: Makes one clear recommendation: ban the assistants, or allow them with rules (either can earn full marks when justified)
Links the recommendation to the incident: the flaw reached customers because AI-generated code was committed unread and wasn't reviewed before release

Explains how the chosen option stops this happening again, e.g. a rule that every AI-generated change is read, tested and approved by a second developer before it is merged; or, for a ban, blocking the assistant and still reviewing every change, since human-written code can contain the same flaw

Weighs the other detail in the scenario, e.g. allowing the assistant with rules keeps the hours saved while the team is behind schedule; or a ban accepts slower work because junior developers can't yet check AI output reliably

model:
Sittella Insurance should allow AI coding assistants, with rules. The flaw didn't happen simply because an assistant was used. It happened because a junior developer committed code without reading it, and nobody reviewed it before release. A ban wouldn't fix that, because a developer's own code could contain the same flaw.

The rules should require every AI-generated function to be marked in a comment, read and understood by the developer who commits it, and tested and approved by a second developer before it is merged, with extra care for code that controls which customers can see which claims. Developers must also never paste customer data into the assistant.

Allowing the assistant with these rules keeps the several hours a week each developer saves, which the team needs while it is behind schedule on the claims app, and it closes the gap that let the flaw reach customers.
mistake: Listing both options without choosing, or choosing without a reason, doesn't answer a 'recommend' question. Commit to one option and tie each reason to the incident and to the schedule.
